facts.fact: In a water supply, an air gap is the open vertical space through free air between the lowest point of the faucet or pipe that fills a fixture or tank and the flood level rim of that receptacle. It is the most reliable way to prevent backflow.

In a drainage system, an air gap is the open vertical space through free air between the outlet of a waste pipe and the flood level rim of the receptor it discharges into, so the waste pipe never touches the waste in the receptor.

An air break is an indirect waste arrangement where the drain from a fixture, appliance or device discharges into another fixture, receptor or interceptor at a point below that receptor's flood level rim but above its trap seal.
facts.note: Contrast with an air gap, where the outlet ends above the flood level rim.

facts.fact: Backflow is any flow of water or other liquids, mixtures or substances into the potable water distribution piping from a source other than its intended source. It happens either by backsiphonage (negative or sub-atmospheric pressure in the supply) or by back pressure (downstream pressure higher than supply pressure).
A branch interval is a vertical length of soil or waste stack, roughly one story high but not less than 8 ft, within which the horizontal branches from one floor connect to the stack.

The building drain is the lowest piping that collects the discharge of all other drainage piping inside the building and carries it to the building sewer, which begins 30 in outside the exterior wall of the building.

The building sewer is the part of the drainage system that runs from the end of the building drain to the public sewer, private sewer, individual sewage disposal system (septic) or other point of disposal.

A cross connection is any physical connection or arrangement between a potable water system and a separate system containing water of questionable safety, steam, gas or chemicals, where flow could pass from one to the other depending on the pressure difference.
A dead end is a branch off a soil, waste or vent pipe, building drain or building sewer that ends with a plug, cap or other closed fitting at a developed length of 2 ft or more.
Developed length is the length of a pipe run measured along the centerline of the pipe and its fittings, not the straight-line distance between the ends.
The flood level rim is the edge of a receptacle (fixture, tank or receptor) from which water overflows. Air gaps, vent heights and vacuum breaker heights are all measured from it.
A horizontal pipe is any pipe or fitting installed at an angle of less than 45 degrees from horizontal. A vertical pipe is any pipe or fitting installed at 45 degrees or more from horizontal.

A stack vent is the extension of a soil or waste stack above the highest horizontal drain connected to it. A vent stack is a separate vertical vent pipe installed mainly to circulate air to and from the drainage system.
facts.note: Students often confuse these two terms.

facts.fact: A wet vent is a vent pipe that also carries waste discharge from other fixtures. A common vent is one vent connecting at the junction of two fixture drains (or to a fixture branch) that serves as the vent for both fixtures.
A circuit vent is a vent that connects to a horizontal drainage branch and vents from two up to eight traps or trapped fixtures connected in a battery.

A relief vent provides air circulation between the drainage and vent systems. A yoke vent is a pipe that connects upward from a soil or waste stack to a vent stack to prevent pressure changes in the stacks.
Tempered water is water with a temperature between 85 F and 110 F.
Under the IPC, gray water is waste water discharged from lavatories, bathtubs, showers, clothes washers and laundry trays. It does not include water closet, urinal, kitchen sink or dishwasher waste.

Clear-water waste includes cooling water and condensate from refrigeration and air-conditioning equipment, cooled steam condensate, cooled boiler blowdown, and other water used without appreciably adding oil, solvents, acids or similar contaminants.
An indirect waste pipe does not connect directly to the drainage system. It discharges through an air break or air gap into a trap, fixture, receptor or interceptor.

The water service pipe runs from the water main or other potable source (or from the meter when the meter is at the public right-of-way) to the building's water distribution system. The water distribution system is the piping that carries water from the service to fixtures, appliances and other outlets.

'Ready access' means you can reach the item without removing a panel, door or similar obstruction and without a portable ladder or step stool. Plain 'access' allows first removing or moving a panel or similar obstruction.

The effective opening is the smallest cross-sectional area at the point where water discharges, expressed as the diameter of a circle (or of a circle with the same area if the opening isn't round). Air gap sizes are based on it.

A sump is a tank or pit below the normal grade of the gravity system that receives sewage or liquid waste and must be emptied mechanically. A building subdrain is the part of the drainage system that cannot drain by gravity into the building sewer.
The trap seal is the vertical distance between the trap weir (crown) and the top of the trap's dip. This water column blocks sewer gas.
facts.note: Required depth is covered separately (2 in to 4 in).

facts.fact: A bathroom group is a water closet, lavatory, and bathtub or shower located together on the same floor, with or without a bidet and/or an emergency floor drain.
A soil pipe carries sewage containing fecal matter. A waste pipe carries only liquid waste free of fecal matter.
An offset is a combination of approved fittings that moves one section of pipe out of line and into a line parallel with the original section.

The critical level is a point on a backflow preventer or vacuum breaker, marked by the manufacturer, that sets its minimum mounting height above the flood level rim or highest downstream outlet. Where no mark is given, the bottom of the device is the critical level.

Contamination (high hazard) is impairment of potable water that creates an actual health hazard through poisoning or disease. Pollution (low hazard) affects the water's looks, taste or odor but does not create a health hazard.
facts.note: Degree of hazard decides which backflow device is allowed.

facts.fact: A pipe passing through a foundation wall needs either a relieving arch or a pipe sleeve built into the wall. The sleeve must be two pipe sizes larger than the pipe passing through it.

Exterior water supply piping must be buried at least 6 in below the frost line and at least 12 in below grade. Water, soil and waste piping may not be run in attics, crawl spaces, outside walls or other freezing locations unless protected by insulation, heat or both.
The model IPC leaves minimum building sewer depth below grade blank for each jurisdiction to fill in (both at the septic tank connection and generally). Check the local amendment for the number.
facts.note: Local value; not a fixed national number.

facts.fact: Where concealed piping (other than cast iron or galvanized steel) passes through holes or notches less than 1-1/2 in from the edge of a stud, joist or rafter, it must be protected by steel shield plates at least 0.0575 in thick (No. 16 gauge). The plates must extend at least 2 in above sole plates and below top plates.
facts.note: The IFGC requires 4 in extension for gas piping.

facts.fact: Buried piping must be supported along its entire length.

Where rock is found in a trench, it must be removed to at least 3 in below the pipe's installed level, and the space backfilled with sand, fine gravel or other approved material. An over-dug trench must be brought back to grade with compacted earth, sand, fine gravel or similar material.

Trench backfill must be free of construction debris, rocks, broken concrete and frozen chunks. Loose earth goes in 6 in layers, tamped until the crown of the pipe is covered by 12 in of tamped earth, and it must be brought up evenly on both sides so the pipe stays aligned.
Where pipe is installed by tunneling, the tunnel must have at least 2 ft of clear height above the pipe. Its length is limited to one-half the trench depth, with a maximum of 8 ft.
A trench running parallel to a footing or wall may not extend into the footing's bearing plane. That plane is a line sloping downward at 45 degrees from the outside bottom edge of the footing.

Plumbing installers may not weaken structural members beyond code limits. Cutting, notching and boring of framing must follow the IBC (or the IRC for dwellings), and trusses may not be cut or altered without an approved engineered design.

In a load-bearing wood stud wall, a notch may not exceed 25% of the stud width and a bored hole may not exceed 40% of the stud width (60% if studs are doubled and no more than two successive studs are bored). Holes must be at least 5/8 in from the stud edge.
facts.note: IRC limit commonly referenced on plumbing exams; IBC 2308 has similar rules.

facts.fact: In a non-bearing wood stud wall, a notch may be up to 40% of the stud width and a bored hole up to 60% of the stud width, at least 5/8 in from the edge.

In sawn lumber floor joists, notches may not exceed one-sixth of the joist depth and are not allowed in the middle third of the span. Bored holes may not exceed one-third of the joist depth and must be at least 2 in from the top or bottom edge.
Toilet facilities must be provided for construction workers and kept sanitary. Nonsewer (portable) construction toilets must comply with ANSI Z4.3.

An air-conditioning condensate drain must be at least 3/4 in inside diameter and may not get smaller from the drain pan to the point of disposal. Horizontal runs need a uniform slope of at least 1/8 in per ft (1%).
Condensate drain size by equipment capacity: up to 20 tons, 3/4 in; 21 to 40 tons, 1 in; 41 to 90 tons, 1-1/4 in; 91 to 125 tons, 1-1/2 in; 126 to 250 tons, 2 in.
The permit holder must notify the code official when work is ready for test and must supply the equipment, materials, power and labor for the inspection and test.

Test gauge increments: tests at 10 psi or less need a gauge reading in 0.10 psi increments or finer; tests over 10 psi up to 100 psi need 1 psi increments or finer; tests over 100 psi need 2 psi increments or finer.
facts.note: Confirmed from Ohio's 2021-based code, which keeps the model values.

facts.fact: DWV rough-in water test: fill each section with at least a 10 ft head of water and hold it for at least 15 minutes. When testing in sections, include at least the upper 10 ft of the section below so every joint gets tested under 10 ft of head.
DWV air test: pump the system to 5 psi (or enough to balance a 10 in column of mercury) and hold it for at least 15 minutes. Plastic piping may not be tested with air under the IPC.
facts.note: Some states (e.g., Ohio) amend this to allow air testing of plastic with safeguards.

facts.fact: The final DWV test, after fixtures are set and traps filled, may be a smoke test or a manometer test. The manometer method requires holding at least a 1 in water column for 15 minutes.

Water supply piping is tested with water at not less than the system's working pressure, or (for piping other than plastic) with air at not less than 50 psi. Either test must hold for at least 15 minutes.
A gravity building sewer is tested by plugging the end at the public sewer connection, filling it with water to at least a 10 ft head, and holding for 15 minutes.
A forced (pumped) sewer is tested at a pressure at least 5 psi greater than the pump rating, held for at least 15 minutes.

A site-built shower liner is tested by plugging the drain and filling the pan with water at least 2 in deep at the threshold (building a temporary dam if the threshold is lower). The water must stand for at least 15 minutes with no leaks.
Testable backflow assemblies (RPZ, double check, pressure vacuum breaker and similar) must be tested at installation, immediately after repair or relocation, and at least once a year.
PVC and ABS pipe need horizontal support at least every 4 ft and vertical support at least every 10 ft, with a mid-story guide for sizes 2 in and smaller.
Cast-iron pipe needs horizontal support every 5 ft (increased to 10 ft where 10-ft lengths are installed) and vertical support every 15 ft.
Copper tubing 1-1/4 in and smaller needs horizontal support every 6 ft. Copper tubing 1-1/2 in and larger needs it every 10 ft. Vertical support for copper tubing is every 10 ft.
facts.note: UPC breaks copper at 1-1/2 in and smaller instead.

facts.fact: Copper or copper-alloy pipe (threaded-pipe dimensions, not tubing) needs horizontal support every 12 ft and vertical support every 10 ft. Brass pipe needs 10 ft both ways.

PEX pipe 1 in and smaller needs horizontal support every 32 in (2.67 ft). PEX 1-1/4 in and larger needs it every 4 ft. Vertical support for PEX is every 10 ft, with a mid-story guide for 2 in and smaller.

CPVC pipe or tubing 1 in and smaller needs horizontal support every 3 ft. CPVC 1-1/4 in and larger needs it every 4 ft. Vertical support for CPVC is every 10 ft, with a mid-story guide for 2 in and smaller.
Steel pipe needs horizontal support every 12 ft and vertical support every 15 ft. Aluminum tubing needs 10 ft horizontal and 15 ft vertical.
PEX-AL-PEX, PE-AL-PE and polybutylene pipe need horizontal support every 32 in and vertical support every 4 ft. Lead pipe must be supported continuously horizontally and every 4 ft vertically.
Stainless steel drainage piping needs horizontal and vertical support every 10 ft.
For pipe 4 in and larger, rigid sway bracing is required at changes in direction greater than 45 degrees.

Drainage piping must be anchored against axial movement. For pipe larger than 4 in, restraints are required at every change in direction and at changes in diameter of more than two pipe sizes, using braces, blocks or rodding as the coupling maker specifies.
In bundled manifold (parallel) water distribution systems, every hot water pipe bundled with cold or other hot water pipes must be insulated. Bundles follow Table 308.5 support spacing.
facts.note: Listed as a 2021 significant change.

facts.fact: Minimum fixture counts come from Table 403.1 using the occupant load from the IBC. The total occupant load is split in half (50% male, 50% female) unless approved data shows otherwise, each fixture ratio is applied to each half, and any fraction is rounded up to the next whole fixture.
facts.note: For mixed occupancies, fractions are summed first, then rounded up.

facts.fact: Business occupancies (Group B): water closets 1 per 25 for the first 50 people and 1 per 50 for the rest; lavatories 1 per 40 for the first 80 and 1 per 80 for the rest; drinking fountains 1 per 100; 1 service sink.
Mercantile occupancies (Group M, retail stores): water closets 1 per 500; lavatories 1 per 750; drinking fountains 1 per 1,000; 1 service sink.
Restaurants, bars and banquet halls (Group A-2): water closets 1 per 75; lavatories 1 per 200; drinking fountains 1 per 500; 1 service sink.
Educational occupancies (Group E): water closets 1 per 50; lavatories 1 per 50; drinking fountains 1 per 100; 1 service sink.
One- and two-family dwellings need, per dwelling unit, 1 water closet, 1 lavatory, 1 bathtub or shower, 1 kitchen sink, and 1 automatic clothes washer connection.

Worked example, business occupancy with 150 occupants: 75 per sex. Water closets per sex = 50/25 + 25/50 = 2.5, rounded up to 3, so 6 total. Lavatories per sex = 75/40 = 1.9, rounded up to 2, so 4 total.
facts.note: Calculation based on Table 403.1 business ratios.

facts.fact: Separate facilities for each sex are not required in dwelling and sleeping units, in buildings or tenant spaces with a total occupant load (employees plus customers) of 15 or fewer, in mercantile occupancies with 100 or fewer occupants, or in business occupancies with 25 or fewer occupants.
facts.note: 2021 also allows nonseparated multiple-user facilities that meet privacy rules.

facts.fact: Required public and employee toilet facilities (outside of malls) must be no more than one story above or below the space they serve, and the path of travel to them may not exceed 500 ft.
facts.note: Covered and open malls: 300 ft (403.3.4).

facts.fact: A toilet room may not open directly into a room used to prepare food for service to the public.
Restaurants that serve free drinking water in containers do not need drinking fountains. In other occupancies, water dispensers may replace up to 50% of the required drinking fountains.
facts.note: 2021 significant change.

facts.fact: A water closet, urinal, lavatory or bidet must be at least 15 in from its center to any side wall, partition, vanity or obstruction, and at least 30 in center to center from an adjacent fixture when no partition separates them. At least 21 in of clear space is required in front of each.
facts.note: UPC requires 24 in in front.

facts.fact: A water closet compartment must be at least 30 in wide and 60 in deep for a floor-mounted water closet, or at least 30 in wide and 56 in deep for a wall-hung water closet.
In employee and public toilet rooms, the required lavatory must be in the same room as the required water closet.

Each water closet used by the public or employees must be in a separate compartment with walls or partitions and a door for privacy. A single-occupant toilet room with a lockable door is an exception.

Each public or employee urinal needs privacy walls or partitions at least 30 in apart. They start no higher than 12 in above the floor, extend at least 60 in above the floor, and project from the back wall at least 18 in or 6 in past the front lip of the urinal, whichever is greater.
facts.note: 30 in spacing confirmed in 2021 text; other dimensions from the same section.

facts.fact: Water closet floor flanges must be at least 0.125 in thick for brass, 0.25 in for plastic, and 0.25 in (with at least a 2 in caulking depth) for cast iron or galvanized malleable iron. Closet screws and bolts must be brass, and flanges are secured with corrosion-resistant fasteners.

Slip joints are allowed only at the trap inlet, trap outlet and within the trap seal, and they need an approved elastomeric gasket. A fixture with concealed slip joints needs an access panel or utility space at least 12 in in its smallest dimension.
An automatic clothes washer must discharge through an air break into a standpipe or into a laundry sink.
Bathtub waste outlets must be at least 1-1/2 in in diameter with an approved stopper. Starting with the 2021 IPC, bathtubs are no longer required to have overflow outlets.
facts.note: 2021 significant change on overflows.

facts.fact: Water supplied to a bidet must be limited to 110 F by a water-temperature limiting device complying with ASSE 1070/ASME A112.1070/CSA B125.70 or CSA B125.3.
Emergency showers and eyewash stations must comply with ISEA Z358.1. A waste connection is not required for them.

Individual shower valves must be pressure-balance, thermostatic mixing, or combination type (ASSE 1016/ASME A112.1016/CSA B125.16), and the installer must set the high limit stop so outlet water does not exceed 120 F.
facts.note: 2021 also requires the valve be rated for the flow of the installed showerhead.

facts.fact: Hot water to bathtubs and whirlpool tubs must be limited to 120 F by a water-temperature limiting device (ASSE 1070/ASME A112.1070/CSA B125.70 or CSA B125.3), unless a combination tub/shower valve meeting the shower valve rules already provides that protection.
Floor drains must have a drain outlet at least 2 in in diameter.

A domestic food waste disposer must connect to a drain at least 1-1/2 in in diameter. A commercial disposer must be on a drain at least 1-1/2 in and be trapped separately from other fixtures or sink compartments. All disposers need a cold water supply protected against backflow.
Each laundry tray compartment needs a waste outlet at least 1-1/2 in in diameter with a strainer or crossbar.
Lavatory waste outlets must be at least 1-1/4 in in diameter and have a strainer, pop-up stopper, crossbar or similar device.

Lavatories and group wash fixtures in public toilet rooms for customers and visitors must deliver tempered water through an ASSE 1070/ASME A112.1070/CSA B125.70 or CSA B125.3 water-temperature limiting device.
facts.note: 2021 significant change.

facts.fact: Shower waste outlets must be at least 1-1/2 in in diameter. Except in bathtubs, they need removable strainers at least 3 in in diameter with openings at least 1/4 in.
facts.note: UPC requires a 2 in shower trap.

facts.fact: A shower compartment needs at least 900 sq in of interior floor area and at least a 30 in minimum dimension (a 30 in circle must fit), measured at the threshold height and kept clear up to 70 in above the drain. Valves, showerheads, soap dishes and grab bars are excluded from the measurement.
facts.note: UPC requires 1,024 sq in.

facts.fact: Exception to the shower size rule: a shower compartment may have a minimum dimension of 25 in if its floor area is at least 1,300 sq in.
The shower compartment access/exit opening must have a clear, unobstructed finished width of at least 22 in.

Site-built shower pan liners must turn up at least 2 in above the finished threshold, may not be nailed or perforated less than 1 in above the finished threshold, and must slope 1/4 in per ft (2%) toward the drain, sealed watertight to the drain's seepage flange.
Approved shower liner materials include PVC sheet at least 0.040 in thick, CPE sheet at least 0.040 in thick, sheet lead at least 4 lb per sq ft, and sheet copper at least 12 oz per sq ft.
Sinks must have waste outlets at least 1-1/2 in in diameter.
Urinals may replace up to 67% of the required water closets in assembly and educational occupancies, and up to 50% in all other occupancies.
Wall and floor surfaces around a urinal must be smooth, cleanable and nonabsorbent from 2 ft in front of the urinal lip, 4 ft up the wall, and at least 2 ft to each side.
Water closets for public or employee use must have elongated bowls and hinged open-front seats made of smooth, nonabsorbent material.

A 4 in x 3 in closet bend is acceptable. Where a 3 in bend serves a water closet, a 4 in x 3 in flange must receive the fixture horn, and the 4 x 3 connection is not treated as a prohibited reduction in pipe size.
Whirlpool bathtub circulation pumps need access. If the manufacturer does not specify the opening, a field-built access opening must be at least 12 in by 12 in.

Maximum flow rates: showerheads 2.5 gpm at 80 psi; private sink faucets 2.2 gpm at 60 psi; public lavatory faucets (non-metering) 0.5 gpm at 60 psi; public metering lavatory faucets 0.25 gallon per cycle.
facts.note: Private lavatory 2.2 gpm is a separate existing fact.

facts.fact: Maximum water use per flush under the IPC: water closets 1.6 gallons per flushing cycle; urinals 1.0 gallon per flushing cycle.
facts.note: Many states and the UPC green provisions require lower values (1.28 gpf and 0.5 gpf).

facts.fact: Accessible plumbing facilities and fixtures must comply with the IBC (Chapter 11) and ICC A117.1.
An accessible water closet's centerline must be 16 in to 18 in from the side wall or partition (17 in to 19 in in an ambulatory accessible stall).
An accessible water closet seat must be 17 in to 19 in above the finished floor, measured to the top of the seat.
The clearance around an accessible water closet must be at least 60 in wide (measured from the side wall) and at least 56 in deep (measured from the rear wall).

At an accessible water closet, the side-wall grab bar must be at least 42 in long, start no more than 12 in from the rear wall, and extend at least 54 in from the rear wall. The rear-wall grab bar must be at least 36 in long, extending at least 12 in on one side of the toilet centerline and 24 in on the other.
Grab bars must be mounted 33 in to 36 in above the finished floor, measured to the top of the gripping surface.
An accessible lavatory or sink rim (or counter surface, whichever is higher) may be no more than 34 in above the floor, and knee clearance beneath must be at least 27 in high.
Exposed water supply and drain pipes under an accessible lavatory or sink must be insulated or otherwise configured to protect against contact.
An accessible urinal (stall-type or wall-hung) must have its rim no more than 17 in above the finished floor and be at least 13-1/2 in deep.
A wheelchair-accessible drinking fountain spout outlet may be no higher than 36 in above the floor. A drinking fountain for standing persons must have its spout outlet 38 in to 43 in above the floor.
An accessible transfer shower is exactly 36 in by 36 in clear inside. A standard roll-in shower is at least 30 in wide by 60 in deep clear inside with a 60 in wide entry.
An accessible shower needs a hand-held spray unit with a hose at least 59 in long, and the shower must deliver water no hotter than 120 F.
Accessible faucets and controls must be operable with one hand without tight grasping, pinching or twisting of the wrist, using no more than 5 lbf of force.

Where a combination potable water heating and space heating system needs water hotter than 140 F for space heating, a master thermostatic mixing valve (ASSE 1017) must limit the water sent to the potable hot water system to 140 F or less.
facts.note: ASSE 1017 reference updated in 2021.

facts.fact: Water from a tankless water heater intended for domestic use may not exceed 140 F. This does not replace the requirement for protective (anti-scald) shower valves.

A water heater with an ignition source installed in a garage must be elevated so the ignition source is at least 18 in above the floor. Water heaters listed as flammable vapor ignition resistant (FVIR) are exempt from the elevation rule.
facts.note: Also protect from vehicle impact.

facts.fact: A water heater in an attic needs an unobstructed passageway at least 30 in high and 22 in wide, no more than 20 ft long, with continuous solid flooring at least 24 in wide. A level service space at least 30 in by 30 in is required at the front, and the access opening must be at least 20 in by 30 in and large enough to remove the heater.
Where earthquake loads apply under the IBC, water heater supports must be designed and installed for seismic forces per the IBC. The IPC itself does not prescribe strap locations.
facts.note: See the UPC strapping rule for specific strap locations.

facts.fact: The cold water line to each water heater or hot water storage tank needs a shutoff valve located near the equipment and serving only that equipment.
Storage water heaters must be protected against siphoning, for example by a cold water dip tube with a hole near the top or a vacuum relief valve in the cold supply above the top of the heater.
Bottom-fed tank-type water heaters, and bottom-fed tanks connected to water heaters, need a vacuum relief valve complying with ANSI Z21.22.

Every storage water heater operating above atmospheric pressure needs an approved self-closing (levered) pressure relief and temperature relief valve, or a combination T&P valve, complying with ANSI Z21.22. The relief valve may not be used to control thermal expansion.

The temperature relief valve must be in the tank shell, placed so the water in the top 6 in of the tank operates it. No check valve or shutoff valve is allowed between the relief valve and the heater or tank.
A water heater relief valve may be set no higher than the heater's rated working pressure or 150 psi, whichever is less.

Relief valve discharge piping may not connect directly to the drainage system. It must discharge through an air gap in the same room as the water heater, be no smaller than the valve outlet (full size to the air gap), and serve only one relief device.

Relief valve discharge piping must not be trapped, must flow by gravity, may have no valves or tee fittings, may not have a threaded outlet end, and must end where building occupants can readily see it, without causing injury or damage.
facts.note: Termination height near the floor is a separate existing fact.

facts.fact: Relief valve discharge may go to the floor, to the water heater pan, to a waste receptor, or to the outdoors. The piping must be a material listed in Section 605.4 or tested and approved under ASME A112.4.1.

A storage tank-type water heater installed where leakage would cause damage must sit in a pan of galvanized steel or aluminum at least 0.0236 in thick, plastic at least 0.036 in thick, or another approved material.
A plastic drain pan may not be installed under a gas-fired water heater.
facts.note: Recalled from 2018/2021 IPC 504.7 text, but not confirmed in a source this round.

facts.fact: A water heater pan must be at least 1-1/2 in deep and drained by an indirect waste pipe at least 3/4 in in diameter.

The pan drain must run full size and end over a suitable indirect waste receptor or floor drain, or extend outdoors and end 6 in to 24 in above the ground. A replacement water heater does not need a pan drain if none was installed before.

Under the UPC, in Seismic Design Categories C through F, a water heater must be anchored or strapped in the upper one-third and lower one-third of its height, with the lower strap at least 4 in above the controls.
facts.note: The IPC only references IBC seismic design without giving strap locations.

facts.fact: Under the UPC, a relief valve drain from a heater inside the building typically runs to the outdoors and ends 6 in to 2 ft above the ground, pointing down. No part may be trapped or exposed to freezing, and the end may not be threaded.
facts.note: The UPC also prohibits ending the drain in a crawl space. That detail was not re-confirmed this round.

facts.fact: The water service pipe must be sized for the flow and pressure the building needs, and it may never be smaller than 3/4 in in diameter.
The water service pipe and building sewer must be separated by at least 5 ft of undisturbed or compacted earth.
facts.note: Exceptions are covered in a separate fact.

facts.fact: Exceptions to the 5 ft water/sewer separation: (1) the bottom of the water pipe is at least 12 in above the top of the sewer and the sewer is a Table 702.3 material; (2) the water service may share the trench with a sewer built of Table 702.2 (inside-building underground) materials; (3) where the water service crosses the sewer, it is sleeved at least 5 ft horizontally on both sides of the sewer centerline.
Potable water service pipe may not be installed in, under or above a cesspool, septic tank, septic drainage field or seepage pit.

Table 604.3 sets the minimum flow rate and flowing pressure each fixture supply outlet must receive. Many fixtures (lavatories, sinks, hose bibbs) need 8 psi flowing pressure, tank-type water closets, bathtubs and showers need 20 psi, and flushometer valves need more.
facts.note: Exact gpm/psi values changed between editions (for example, the lavatory dropped to 0.8 gpm, and flushometer pressures were raised). The 8 psi / 20 psi pattern was not checked against the 2021 table.

facts.fact: Minimum fixture supply pipe sizes: lavatory 3/8 in; water closet flush tank 3/8 in; bathtub 1/2 in; shower 1/2 in; kitchen sink 1/2 in; hose bibb 1/2 in; urinal flush valve 3/4 in; water closet flush valve 1 in.
A fixture supply pipe must end no more than 30 in from its connection point at the fixture. A reduced-size flexible connector between the supply pipe and fixture must be an approved type.
Where street main pressure fluctuates, the building water distribution system must be designed for the minimum pressure available.
A pressure-reducing valve must be designed to stay open so water keeps flowing if the valve fails, and it must be installed with unions, flanges or similar fittings so it can be repaired or removed.
facts.note: The 80 psi trigger for a PRV is a separate existing fact.

facts.fact: Water velocity must be controlled to reduce water hammer, and a water-hammer arrestor (ASSE 1010) is required where quick-closing valves are used, installed per the manufacturer's instructions.
Pipe, fittings, valves, faucets and fixture fittings that supply water for drinking or cooking must comply with NSF 372, with a weighted average lead content of 0.25% or less.
facts.note: Matches the federal Reduction of Lead in Drinking Water Act.

facts.fact: Joints in water supply piping must use lead-free solder and flux. 'Lead-free' solder means no more than 0.2% lead.
facts.note: 2021 also requires solder and flux to conform to NSF 61.

facts.fact: PVC pipe is approved for underground water service (Table 605.3) but not for water distribution inside a building (Table 605.4). CPVC, PEX, copper, PE-RT and others are approved for distribution.
Copper water tube Types K, L and M (ASTM B88) are all approved for water distribution under the IPC. Type K has the thickest wall and Type M the thinnest.
facts.note: Some local codes restrict Type M.

facts.fact: Prohibited water supply joints and connections include cement or concrete joints, mastic or hot-poured bituminous joints, solvent-cement joints between different types of plastic, and saddle-type fittings.

Full-open valves are required on the water service near the curb, at the building entrance, on the discharge side of every water meter, at the base of risers (except in small residential), at the top of down-feed pipes (except 1- and 2-family), at the entrance to each dwelling unit, on the supply to a gravity or pressure tank, and on the supply to every water heater.
facts.note: 2021 added an individual tenant shutoff requirement.

facts.fact: Shutoff valves are required on the supply to each fixture (except bathtubs and showers in 1- and 2-family homes and in hotel units with unit shutoffs), on the supply to each sillcock, and on the supply to each appliance or piece of mechanical equipment.
A water pressure booster pump needs a low-pressure cutoff that stops the pump when suction-side pressure drops to 10 psi or less, preventing a vacuum on the suction side.

Residential occupancies must supply hot water to all fixtures and equipment used for bathing, washing, cooking, cleaning, laundry and building maintenance. Nonresidential occupancies must supply hot or tempered water for bathing and washing, with tempered water limited to 110 F by an ASSE 1070 device.
A water heater's thermostat may not serve as the water-temperature limiting device for tempered or temperature-limited water.
The developed length of hot or tempered water piping from the hot water source to a fixture may not exceed 50 ft. A recirculating loop or heat-traced pipe counts as the source.

Where cold water to a storage water heater passes through a check valve, pressure-reducing valve or backflow preventer (a closed system), a thermal expansion control device must be installed on the heater's cold supply downstream of those devices. It must be sized to keep system pressure within the 80 psi limit.
Faucets and diverters must be installed so hot water comes from the left side of the fixture fitting.
Temperature-actuated (thermostatic) mixing valves used to reduce water temperature for the distribution system must comply with ASSE 1017 and be installed at the hot water source.
facts.note: ASSE 1017 is the master mixing valve. ASSE 1070 is for point-of-use limiting at fixtures. ASSE 1016 is for shower valves.

facts.fact: Common hot water temperature limits in the IPC: showers and bathtubs 120 F max; tempered water, bidets and public hand-washing 110 F max; tankless domestic water and ASSE 1017 master valve output 140 F max.
facts.note: Summary of separate code sections.

facts.fact: The potable water supply must be protected against backflow from every fixture, device and connection, using a method appropriate to the degree of hazard and the type of backflow (backsiphonage or back pressure).

Air gaps are measured vertically from the lowest end of the potable water outlet to the flood level rim of the receptacle, and are never less than 1 in. For effective openings larger than 1 in, the gap must be at least twice the opening diameter away from walls, or three times the diameter where walls are close to the outlet.

Minimum air gaps away from a wall (near a wall): lavatories, openings up to 1/2 in: 1 in (1-1/2 in). Sinks, laundry trays and gooseneck faucets, openings up to 3/4 in: 1-1/2 in (2-1/2 in). Over-rim bath fillers, openings up to 1 in: 2 in (3 in). Drinking fountain orifices up to 7/16 in: 1 in (1-1/2 in).
A reduced pressure principle backflow preventer (RPZ, ASSE 1013) protects against both back pressure and backsiphonage, and is approved for high hazard (contamination) as well as low hazard.
A double check valve assembly (DCVA, ASSE 1015) protects against both back pressure and backsiphonage, but only for low hazard (pollution) conditions.

A pressure vacuum breaker assembly (PVB, ASSE 1020) protects only against backsiphonage, for high or low hazard. Unlike an atmospheric vacuum breaker, it may be under continuous pressure with valves downstream.
facts.note: Spill-resistant vacuum breakers are ASSE 1056.

facts.fact: An atmospheric vacuum breaker (AVB, ASSE 1001) protects only against backsiphonage. It may not be under continuous pressure, so no shutoff valve may be installed downstream. It must be installed with its critical level at least 6 in above the flood level rim or highest downstream outlet.
Hose bibbs and other threaded hose outlets must be protected by a hose connection vacuum breaker (such as ASSE 1011) or another approved device, because a hose can be submerged in contaminated water.
A barometric loop protects only against backsiphonage. It must rise at least 35 ft above the highest outlet and come before the point of connection.

The potable supply to a boiler needs a backflow preventer with an intermediate atmospheric vent (ASSE 1012 or CSA B64.3). If chemical conditioners are added to the boiler water, a reduced pressure principle backflow preventer (RPZ) is required.
facts.note: Low-hazard boiler device listed as a 2021 significant change.

facts.fact: Lawn irrigation supplies need an atmospheric vacuum breaker, pressure vacuum breaker, spill-resistant vacuum breaker or RPZ. No valve may be installed downstream of an AVB. If chemicals (fertilizer) are injected, an RPZ is required.

The potable supply to automatic fire sprinkler and standpipe systems needs a double check (or double check fire protection) assembly, or an RPZ (or RPZ fire protection) assembly. If antifreeze or other additives are used, or the system can connect to a nonpotable source, an RPZ is required.
facts.note: Residential multipurpose systems with no fire department connection are exempt from isolation.

facts.fact: The water supply to a carbonated beverage dispenser must be protected by an ASSE 1022 backflow preventer or an air gap. Piping downstream of the device must not be affected by carbon dioxide gas, so copper is not used there.
facts.note: CO2 mixed with water forms carbonic acid that dissolves copper.

facts.fact: Heat exchangers using a nonpotable or toxic transfer fluid must be double-wall with a leak path to the atmosphere. Single-wall construction is allowed only when the transfer fluid is potable water or an essentially nontoxic fluid.

Potable water outlets and combination stop-and-waste valves may not be installed underground or below grade. A freezeproof yard hydrant that drains into the ground counts as a stop-and-waste valve, unless its supply is protected upstream by a backflow preventer and it is labeled as nonpotable.

The relief port discharge from a reduced pressure principle backflow preventer must go through an air gap, and the installation must be arranged so relief discharge does not flood the area or submerge the device.
facts.note: 2021 added rules for relief opening discharge (608.15.2.1). Exact wording and location limits not confirmed.

facts.fact: New or repaired potable water systems must be flushed until clean water appears, then disinfected with either at least 50 ppm (mg/L) chlorine held 24 hours, or at least 200 ppm chlorine held 3 hours. The system is then flushed until the chlorine is purged.

If a bacteriological test after disinfection shows contamination remains, the disinfection procedure must be repeated. The health authority or water purveyor's method, or AWWA C651/C652, may be used instead of the code's procedure.
Reverse osmosis drinking water treatment units must discharge their waste to the drainage system through an air gap or an air gap device (NSF 58).
Horizontal drainage pipe 8 in and larger needs a minimum slope of 1/16 in per ft (0.5%).
facts.note: Smaller sizes are covered by existing facts (1/4 in/ft for 2-1/2 in and less, 1/8 in/ft for 3 to 6 in).

facts.fact: Drainage piping may not be reduced in size in the direction of flow. A 4 in by 3 in water closet connection is not considered a reduction.

Horizontal branches must connect to the base of a stack, or to a horizontal stack offset, at least 10 times the stack diameter downstream of the stack. For example, a 4 in stack means at least 40 in downstream.

A sanitary tee may be used only for a change in direction from horizontal to vertical, such as a horizontal fixture drain entering a vertical stack. It may not be used vertical to horizontal or horizontal to horizontal.

Wyes, combination wye and eighth bends, long-sweep quarter bends, and sixteenth, eighth and sixth bends are allowed for all three changes of direction: horizontal to vertical, vertical to horizontal, and horizontal to horizontal.

A double sanitary tee (double tee) may not receive the discharge of back-to-back water closets or of fixtures with pumping-action discharge. Back-to-back water closets may use a double sanitary tee only if the horizontal developed length from each closet outlet to the fitting is 18 in or more.
Drainage fittings may not have ledges, shoulders or reductions that slow or block flow, and threaded drainage fittings must be the recessed drainage (Durham) type.

Prohibited drainage joints and connections include cement or concrete joints, mastic or hot-poured bituminous joints, joints between different diameter pipes made with elastomeric rolling O-rings, solvent-cement joints between different types of plastic, saddle-type fittings, and fittings not approved for the installation.
Solvent-cemented PVC joints require a purple primer (ASTM F656) followed by a solvent cement that conforms to ASTM D2564 or CSA B137.3 and is not purple.
facts.note: The IPC has an exception allowing no primer on nonpressure PVC DWV up to 4 in where the cement is third-party certified to ASTM D2564. Confirm the local adoption.

facts.fact: Common above-ground DWV pipe materials include PVC (ASTM D2665, Schedule 40 solid wall or ASTM F891 cellular core), ABS (ASTM D2661 or F628), cast iron (ASTM A74, A888 or CISPI 301), copper Type DWV, galvanized steel and stainless steel.

Drainage fixture unit (DFU) values: bathtub 2; shower (5.7 gpm or less) 2; domestic kitchen sink 2 (still 2 with a disposer and/or dishwasher); domestic dishwasher 2; residential clothes washer 2; laundry tray 2; service sink 2; bidet 1; drinking fountain 1/2.
facts.note: Lavatory (1 DFU) is a separate existing fact.

facts.fact: Water closet DFU values: private 1.6 gpf = 3; public 1.6 gpf = 4; private flushing more than 1.6 gpf = 4; public flushing more than 1.6 gpf = 6; flushometer tank (public or private) = 4.
A bathroom group with a 1.6 gpf water closet is 5 DFU, and 6 DFU with a water closet flushing more than 1.6 gpf. Fixtures added to the group are added to that count.

Urinal DFU values: standard urinal 4; urinal flushing 1 gallon or less 2; nonwater-supplied (waterless) urinal 1/2. A commercial clothes washer is 3 DFU with a 2 in trap. A floor drain is 2 DFU (2 in trap). An emergency floor drain is 0 DFU.

Shower DFU values depend on total flow through all showerheads and body sprays: 5.7 gpm or less = 2 DFU (1-1/2 in trap); over 5.7 to 12.3 gpm = 3 (2 in trap); over 12.3 to 25.8 gpm = 5 (3 in trap); over 25.8 to 55.6 gpm = 6 (4 in trap).

Minimum trap sizes: lavatory 1-1/4 in; bidet 1-1/4 in; drinking fountain 1-1/4 in; bathtub 1-1/2 in; kitchen sink 1-1/2 in; laundry tray 1-1/2 in; service sink 1-1/2 in; clothes washer standpipe 2 in; floor drain 2 in.
For fixtures not listed in Table 709.1, DFU is based on trap or fixture drain size: 1-1/4 in or less = 1; 1-1/2 in = 2; 2 in = 3; 2-1/2 in = 4; 3 in = 5; 4 in = 6.
Continuous or semicontinuous flow into a drainage system (for example, a pump or AC unit) is counted as 2 DFU for each 1 gpm of flow.
Waste receptors (floor drains, floor sinks, hub drains) that receive only clear-water waste are rated at one-half DFU.

Building drain and building sewer capacity (DFU) at 1/8 in per ft / 1/4 in per ft / 1/2 in per ft: 3 in = 36 / 42 / 50; 4 in = 180 / 216 / 250; 5 in = 390 / 480 / 575; 6 in = 700 / 840 / 1,000. Pipe 2-1/2 in and smaller is listed only at 1/4 and 1/2 in per ft (2 in: 21 and 26).
An 8 in building drain or sewer can carry 1,400 DFU at 1/16 in per ft, 1,600 at 1/8 in per ft, 1,920 at 1/4 in per ft, and 2,300 at 1/2 in per ft.
Maximum DFU on a horizontal fixture branch: 1-1/2 in = 3; 2 in = 6; 2-1/2 in = 12; 3 in = 20; 4 in = 160; 5 in = 360; 6 in = 620. Branches of the building drain are not included.

Maximum DFU on a stack: a 3 in stack carries 48 DFU with three or fewer branch intervals and 72 DFU with more than three (no more than 20 DFU in one branch interval). A 4 in stack carries 240 and 500 DFU (90 DFU per branch interval).

Worked example: a house with two bathroom groups (1.6 gpf), a kitchen sink and a clothes washer = 5 + 5 + 2 + 2 = 14 DFU. A 3 in building drain at 1/4 in per ft (42 DFU) is adequate. Because a water closet has a 3 in outlet and drains can't be reduced, the building drain can't be smaller than 3 in anyway.
facts.note: Calculation using verified table values.

facts.fact: In buildings of five stories or more, a stack offset of 45 degrees or less from vertical is sized as a straight vertical stack. Horizontal offsets (more than 45 degrees) are sized as building drains and have special venting rules.
Horizontal drainage pipes in buildings and building drains need cleanouts at intervals of no more than 100 ft. Building sewers smaller than 8 in also need cleanouts at least every 100 ft.
facts.note: Values confirmed in 2012 text. 2021 reorganized the subsections under 708.1.

facts.fact: Building sewers 8 in and larger use manholes instead of cleanouts: one within 200 ft of the building drain/sewer junction, at each change in direction, and at intervals of no more than 400 ft. Manholes serving a building drain need secured gas-tight covers.

A cleanout is required at each change of direction greater than 45 degrees in the building sewer, building drain and horizontal waste or soil lines. Where a run has more than one change of direction, only one cleanout is required for each 40 ft of developed length.

A cleanout is required near the junction of the building drain and building sewer, inside or outside the wall, brought up to grade or the basement floor. One approved two-way cleanout can serve both. It isn't required if a cleanout on a 3 in or larger soil stack is within 10 ft of developed length from the junction.
Cleanouts must be the same nominal size as the pipe they serve up to 4 in. For pipe larger than 4 in, the cleanout must be at least 4 in.
Cleanouts on 6 in and smaller pipe need at least 18 in of clearance for rodding. Cleanouts on 8 in and larger pipe need at least 36 in.
Cleanouts must open in the direction of flow or at right angles to it. They must be accessible and may not be concealed, and cleanout openings may not be used to connect new fixtures unless approved.
Under the 2021 IPC, a fixture trap that can be removed without disturbing concealed piping may serve as a cleanout in some cases.
facts.note: Listed as a 2021 significant change ('removable fixture traps serving as cleanouts'). Exact conditions not confirmed.

facts.fact: Building subdrains that can't drain to the sewer by gravity must discharge into a tightly covered, vented sump, with automatic pumping equipment lifting the waste into the gravity drainage system. In new buildings, the sump may not receive drainage from any piping that could flow by gravity to the sewer.

A sump pump or sewage ejector discharge needs a check valve, plus a full-open valve on the discharge side of the check valve. Both must be accessible, located above the sump cover (or in an access pit if the discharge is below grade).
A sump pit must be at least 18 in in diameter and at least 24 in deep unless otherwise approved, with a solid bottom that supports the pump, a gastight removable cover, and a vent per Chapter 9.
The sump's effluent level control must keep effluent from rising to within 2 in of the invert of the gravity drain inlet into the sump.
Where a pump discharge connects to horizontal drainage piping, it must enter through a wye fitting into the top of the drain, at least 10 pipe diameters from the base of any stack or fixture drain.

Sewage pumps and ejectors receiving water closet discharge must handle spherical solids up to 2 in in diameter. Other pumps must handle solids up to 1 in. Minimum capacity by discharge pipe size: 2 in = 21 gpm; 2-1/2 in = 30 gpm; 3 in = 46 gpm.
facts.note: Grinder pumps and macerating units are exceptions.

facts.fact: Fixtures on a floor lower than the manhole cover of the next upstream public sewer manhole must be protected by a backwater valve. Fixtures on floors above that elevation may not discharge through the backwater valve.
facts.note: In existing buildings, upper fixtures are not prohibited from discharging through it.

facts.fact: Backwater valves must provide a positive mechanical seal against backflow, be at least the same diameter as the pipe they serve, and be accessible for service.
Food-handling equipment (such as refrigerators, steam tables, ice machines and similar) must discharge through indirect waste, not directly to the drainage system.
Devices discharging potable clear water (such as sterilizers and relief valves), plus swimming pool filter backwash and pool deck drains, must discharge indirectly through an air gap.

A domestic dishwasher may drain through an air gap or air break into a standpipe or waste receptor, or into a wye on the sink tailpiece or the disposer inlet. In the tailpiece or disposer case, it must go through a deck-mounted air gap, or the drain hose must rise and be fastened to the underside of the counter (high loop).
A commercial dishwashing machine must discharge through an air gap or air break into a standpipe or waste receptor. Food utensil, dish, pot and pan sinks also discharge indirectly.

Indirect waste piping discharges through an air gap or air break into a trapped and vented waste receptor or standpipe. An indirect waste pipe longer than 30 in horizontal developed length, or 54 in total developed length, must itself be trapped.
An indirect waste air gap must be at least twice the effective opening of the indirect waste pipe, measured to the flood level rim of the receptor.

Waste receptors need a removable strainer or basket (except hub drains for clear water, and standpipes). They must be in ventilated, accessible spaces, and may not be installed in bathrooms, toilet rooms, closets or storerooms.
A hub drain must be a hub or pipe extending at least 1 in above a water-impervious floor.
A standpipe (such as a clothes washer standpipe) must be individually trapped and extend at least 18 in but no more than 42 in above the trap weir, with access to the trap for rodding.
facts.note: Value confirmed. 2021 subsection number not confirmed.

facts.fact: Steam pipes may not connect to the drainage system, and water above 140 F may not discharge directly into it. Such discharge must go to an indirect waste receptor.
Corrosive liquids, spent acids and harmful chemicals must be diluted, neutralized or treated (for example, by a neutralizing tank) before entering the plumbing system.
The vent system must let air in and out so no fixture trap seal is exposed to a pneumatic pressure differential of more than 1 in of water column.
The plumbing vent system may be used only for venting the plumbing system, not for any other purpose.

The model IPC leaves the height that open vent pipes must extend above the roof for each jurisdiction to fill in. Where the roof is used for assembly, as a promenade, observation deck or sunbathing deck, vents must end at least 7 ft above the roof.
facts.note: IRC and UPC use 6 in for ordinary roofs.

facts.fact: Where the 97.5% winter design temperature is 0 F or colder, vent extensions through a roof or wall must be at least 3 in in diameter (frost closure protection). Any size increase must be made at least 1 ft inside the building's thermal envelope.
Vent terminals may not be used to support flagpoles, TV aerials or similar items, except as approved.

An open vent terminal may not be directly beneath a door, operable window or other air intake, and may not be within 10 ft horizontally of such an opening unless it is at least 3 ft above the top of the opening.

A vent terminal through a side wall must be at least 10 ft from a lot line and at least 10 ft above average ground level. It may not end under an overhang with soffit vents and must be protected against birds and rodents.
Where the 97.5% winter design temperature is below 0 F, vent pipes on the exterior of a building must be protected against freezing by insulation, heat or both.
The vent system serving each building drain must have at least one vent pipe extending to the outdoors.
A vent stack is required for every drainage stack that has five or more branch intervals.

A vent stack must connect to the base of the drainage stack at or below the lowest horizontal branch. Where it connects to the building drain instead, the connection must be downstream of the stack within 10 times the stack diameter.
Vent and branch vent pipes must be graded and connected so they drain back to the drainage pipe by gravity.
Every dry vent that connects to a horizontal drain must connect above the centerline of the drain pipe.
Every dry vent must rise vertically to at least 6 in above the flood level rim of the highest trap or trapped fixture it vents before running horizontally.

A vent may connect to a vent stack or stack vent only at least 6 in above the flood level rim of the highest fixture it serves. Horizontal branch, relief or loop vent piping must also be at least 6 in above the flood level rim of the highest fixture served.

Individual, branch, circuit and relief vents must be at least one-half the required diameter of the drain they serve and never smaller than 1-1/4 in. A vent longer than 40 ft in developed length must be increased one nominal pipe size for its entire length.
facts.note: Example: a 3 in drain needs at least a 1-1/2 in vent; a 4 in drain needs 2 in.

facts.fact: Stack vents and vent stacks are sized from Table 906.1 using the drainage stack size, the total DFU connected, and the vent's developed length.
The air-pressure relief pipe from a pneumatic sewage ejector must connect to an independent vent stack terminating like a roof vent, and must be at least 1-1/4 in.
Horizontal offsets in a drainage stack must be vented where five or more branch intervals are above the offset, by venting both the upper and lower sections of the stack.

Soil and waste stacks with more than 10 branch intervals need a relief vent at every tenth interval, counting down from the top floor. The relief vent is the same size as the vent stack. Its lower end connects to the stack through a wye below that floor's horizontal branch, and its upper end connects to the vent stack through a wye at least 3 ft above the floor.

Maximum distance from fixture trap to vent (trap arm), at 1/4 in per ft for 2 in and smaller and 1/8 in per ft for 3 and 4 in: 1-1/4 in trap = 5 ft; 1-1/2 in = 6 ft; 2 in = 8 ft; 3 in = 12 ft; 4 in = 16 ft.
facts.note: UPC trap arm lengths are much shorter.

facts.fact: The total fall of a fixture drain due to its slope may not exceed the diameter of the fixture drain, and except for water closets, the vent connection may not be below the trap weir.
facts.note: Prevents the trap arm from siphoning the trap.

facts.fact: A vent may not be installed within two pipe diameters of the trap weir. Such a 'crown vent' is prohibited.
Any trap or trapped fixture may have an individual vent, which connects to that fixture's drain.

One individual vent may serve two traps as a common vent if the fixtures are on the same floor. If the fixture drains connect at the same level, the vent connects at or downstream of where they join. If at different levels, the vent continues straight up from the vertical drain, and the upper fixture may not be a water closet.
When a common vent serves fixtures at different levels, the vertical drain between them is sized by the upper fixture's discharge: 1-1/2 in pipe = 1 DFU max; 2 in = 4 DFU; 2-1/2 to 3 in = 6 DFU.

Any combination of fixtures within two bathroom groups on the same floor may be vented by a horizontal wet vent. Each wet-vented fixture drain connects independently to the wet vent, and only one wet-vented fixture drain may discharge upstream of the dry-vented connection.
facts.note: ICC describes it as serving 2 to 10 fixtures, with no more than two of any one type.

facts.fact: Wet vent pipe size by DFU load: 1-1/2 in = 1 DFU; 2 in = 4 DFU; 2-1/2 in = 6 DFU; 3 in = 12 DFU.

In a vertical wet vent, water closet drains must connect at the same elevation, other fixture drains connect at or above that elevation, and the water closets are the most downstream fixtures. The dry vent at the top is an individual or common vent serving one or two fixtures.
The dry vent serving a wet vent system is sized at least one-half the diameter of the largest pipe in the wet-vented system.

A waste stack vent lets a vertical waste stack serve as the vent for the fixtures draining into it. The stack may have no offsets between the lowest and highest fixture connections, water closets and urinals may not connect to it, and it is sized from Table 913.4.
facts.note: Vent offsets are allowed only 6 in or more above the highest branch connection.

facts.fact: A circuit vent may serve up to eight fixtures on a horizontal branch drain. Each fixture drain connects horizontally to the branch, and the circuit vent connects between the two most upstream fixture drains.
The vent section of a circuit-vented horizontal branch may slope no more than 1 in per 12 in (8%) and must be sized for the total drainage discharge to the branch.
A relief vent is required on a circuit-vented horizontal branch that receives four or more water closets and connects to a drainage stack that also receives soil or waste from upper branches.

In a combination waste and vent system, the horizontal pipe may slope no more than 1/2 in per ft (4%), and the minimum slope from Table 704.1 still applies. The system needs a dry vent, which rises at least 6 in above the flood level rim of the highest fixture before offsetting horizontally.
facts.note: Fixture types allowed were revised in 2021 (food waste disposers). Check 915.1.

facts.fact: Island fixture venting is limited to sinks and lavatories (residential kitchen sinks with a dishwasher and/or disposer are allowed). The vent must rise above the fixture's drain outlet before offsetting, and cleanouts are required.
Individual and branch-type air admittance valves (AAVs) must comply with ASSE 1051. Stack-type AAVs must comply with ASSE 1050.

Individual and branch AAVs must be at least 4 in above the horizontal branch drain or fixture drain they vent. Stack-type AAVs must be at least 6 in above the flood level rim of the highest fixture vented. All AAVs must be at least 6 in above insulation and within the maximum developed length allowed for the vent.
AAVs only let air in; they don't relieve positive pressure. Every plumbing system must still have at least one stack vent or vent stack extending outdoors to open air.

Stack-type AAVs may not serve as the vent terminal for drainage stacks with more than six branch intervals. A relief vent is required where a horizontal branch using AAVs is more than four branch intervals from the top of the stack.
AAVs must be accessible for replacement and located where air can enter. They may not be in supply or return air plenums, and may not vent sumps or tanks unless engineered for it.
Individual and branch-type AAVs may vent only fixtures that are on the same floor level and connect to a horizontal branch drain.

Each fixture must have its own liquid-seal trap. The vertical distance from the fixture outlet to the trap weir may not exceed 24 in, the horizontal distance from the outlet to the trap inlet may not exceed 30 in, and a fixture may not be double trapped.
A combination fixture (such as a two- or three-compartment sink) may use one trap if no compartment is more than 6 in deeper than another and the waste outlets are no more than 30 in apart.
Fixture traps must be self-scouring and generally may not have interior partitions. Slip joints are allowed only on the trap inlet, trap outlet and within the trap seal.

Prohibited traps: traps that depend on moving parts for the seal, bell traps, crown-vented traps, separate traps that depend on interior partitions (unless made of corrosion-resistant approved material), S-traps, and drum traps (except drum traps used as solids interceptors or on chemical waste systems).

Trap seals of emergency floor drains and other traps that can dry out from evaporation must be protected by a trap primer (potable water-supplied ASSE 1018 or waste water-supplied ASSE 1044), a barrier-type trap seal device (ASSE 1072), or another approved method.
facts.note: 2021 added fixture drains as a priming method (1002.4.1.5).

facts.fact: A fixture trap must be large enough to drain the fixture rapidly and no smaller than Table 709.1 requires. A trap may not be larger than the drainage pipe it discharges into.
Building (house) traps are prohibited, except in special cases where sewer gases are extremely corrosive or noxious and the code official approves.
Traps must be set level with respect to the trap seal and, where needed, protected from freezing.

A grease interceptor or automatic grease removal device is required for fixtures and equipment with grease-laden waste in food prep areas of restaurants, hotel kitchens, hospitals, schools, bars, cafeterias and clubs. Examples include pot sinks, prerinse sinks, soup kettles, wok stations, floor drains or sinks receiving kettle drainage, and hood wash units. Individual dwelling units are exempt.
A food waste disposer may not discharge into a grease interceptor.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2018 IPC. No 2021 change listed.

facts.fact: Hydromechanical grease interceptors are rated by flow (gpm) and sized per ASME A112.14.3, ASME A112.14.6, CSA B481 or PDI G101. A flow control device is required where the interceptor's rating depends on one.

Oil separators are required at repair garages with floor or trench drains, car washes, factories producing oily or flammable waste, and hydraulic elevator pits. All oil-, grease- or flammable-bearing waste goes through the separator before the drainage system.

Where vehicles are serviced, repaired or washed or gasoline is dispensed, an oil separator needs at least 6 cu ft of capacity for the first 100 sq ft drained, plus 1 cu ft for each additional 100 sq ft. Parking garages without servicing, washing or fuel dispensing don't need one.
Worked example: an oil separator for a 1,000 sq ft repair garage floor needs 6 cu ft for the first 100 sq ft plus 9 x 1 cu ft for the remaining 900 sq ft = 15 cu ft minimum.
facts.note: Calculation using the code formula.

facts.fact: Clothes washers in commercial and public laundries must discharge through an interceptor with a removable wire basket or similar device that stops solids 1/2 in or larger, string, rags and buttons. Individual dwelling units are exempt.
Storm water may not be drained into sewers intended only for sanitary sewage.
Vertical conductors, leaders, building storm drains and storm sewers are sized from the 100-year hourly rainfall rate (Figure 1106.1) or approved local weather data.
When sizing roof drains and storm piping, add one-half the area of any vertical wall that diverts rainwater onto the roof to the projected roof area.

Allowable projected roof area for vertical leaders at 1 in per hour of rainfall: 3 in leader = 8,800 sq ft; 4 in leader = 18,400 sq ft. Divide by the design rainfall rate for other rates (4 in leader at 2 in/hr = 9,200 sq ft).

Vertical leader capacity at 1 in per hour: 2 in = 2,880 sq ft (30 gpm); 3 in = 8,800 sq ft (92 gpm); 4 in = 18,400 sq ft (192 gpm); 5 in = 34,600 sq ft (360 gpm); 6 in = 54,000 sq ft (563 gpm); 8 in = 116,000 sq ft (1,208 gpm).
facts.note: 3 in and 4 in confirmed in an older edition. Others from table memory with a stable history.

facts.fact: Storm flow formula: gpm = roof area (sq ft) x rainfall (in/hr) x 0.0104. 1 gpm equals about 96 sq ft of roof at 1 in/hr. Example: 10,000 sq ft at 3 in/hr = 312 gpm.
facts.note: 1 sq ft x 1/12 ft/hr = 0.0833 cu ft/hr x 7.48 = 0.623 gal/hr / 60 = 0.0104 gpm.

facts.fact: Worked example: a 4 in leader handles 18,400 sq ft at 1 in/hr, so at a 3 in/hr design rate it handles 18,400 / 3 = about 6,133 sq ft of roof.
facts.note: Calculation from table values.

facts.fact: Continuous or semicontinuous discharge into a storm drain (pump, ejector, AC unit) is counted as 24 sq ft of roof area for each 1 gpm, based on a 4 in/hr rainfall rate.
facts.note: Check: 24 sq ft x 4 in/hr x 0.0104 = 1 gpm.

facts.fact: Secondary (emergency overflow) roof drains or scuppers are required where parapets or other roof perimeter construction would trap water if the primary drains clog. Secondary drains must discharge separately from the primary system, above grade, where occupants or maintenance staff would notice.

Secondary roof drain systems are sized like the primary system for the same rainfall rate. Scuppers must be sized so ponding doesn't exceed the roof's design depth, and no scupper opening dimension may be less than 4 in.
Roofs must be designed for the maximum possible depth of ponded water, assuming all primary roof drains are blocked.
Roof drain strainers must extend at least 4 in above the surrounding roof surface. Flat-deck strainers on promenade or parking decks must have an inlet area at least two times the drain pipe area.
facts.note: These values are from earlier IPC editions. The 2018/2021 editions revised Section 1105 (roof drains are now tested and rated for flow), so these rules may no longer appear in this form.

facts.fact: Leaders and storm drains connected to a combined sewer must be trapped, either individually at each conductor or with a single trap in the main storm drain before it joins the combined sewer.

Subsoil (foundation) drains must be open-jointed, split or perforated pipe at least 4 in in diameter. They discharge to a trapped area drain, sump, dry well or approved place above ground, and need a backwater valve if subject to backwater. A subsoil sump doesn't need a gastight cover or vent.
Medical gas and medical vacuum piping systems must be installed, tested and labeled per NFPA 99. The 2021 IPC also addresses nonflammable medical gas systems through NFPA 99.

Medical gas piping is typically ASTM B819 copper tube (Type K or L) cleaned for oxygen service. Joints are brazed while purging with nitrogen, and copper-to-copper joints use BCuP brazing alloy without flux.
Installers of medical gas piping systems must be qualified to the ASSE 6010 (Series 6000) professional qualification standard.

Where a nonpotable water system (gray water, rainwater or reclaimed water) gets makeup water from the potable system, the potable supply must be protected by an air gap or a reduced pressure principle backflow preventer.

Nonpotable water piping must be identified (commonly purple for reclaimed and other nonpotable systems) with markings such as 'CAUTION: NONPOTABLE WATER, DO NOT DRINK'. Outlets and fixtures served by nonpotable water need signs.

IPC Chapter 13 covers three kinds of nonpotable systems: on-site nonpotable reuse (including gray water), rainwater collection and distribution, and reclaimed (municipally treated) water. Typical uses are water closet and urinal flushing and irrigation.
Gas piping must be sized and installed to supply each appliance's maximum demand while delivering at least the minimum supply pressure the appliance requires.

Gas demand in cubic feet per hour (cfh) is calculated from the appliance manufacturers' input ratings (Btu/h), adjusted for altitude: cfh = total Btu/h divided by the gas heating value. With natural gas at about 1,000 Btu per cu ft, a 100,000 Btu/h furnace needs about 100 cfh.
facts.note: Get the actual heating value from the gas supplier.

facts.fact: Worked example: furnace 100,000 + water heater 40,000 + range 65,000 Btu/h = 205,000 Btu/h, or about 205 cfh of natural gas at 1,000 Btu per cu ft. Each section of pipe is then sized from the tables for the load it carries.
facts.note: Calculation example.

facts.fact: Gas pipe may be sized from the IFGC tables (Tables 402.4(1) through 402.4(37)), from a listed piping system's manufacturer tables (such as CSST), or by other approved engineering methods. With the tables, pipe length is set by the longest length, branch length or hybrid pressure method.

In the longest length method, each section of gas piping is sized using the total length from the point of delivery (meter or regulator) to the most remote outlet, combined with the load carried by that section.
Inside buildings, gas piping design operating pressure is generally limited to 5 psig, unless specific conditions are met (such as welded piping or certain industrial installations).

Exposed gas piping other than black steel must be identified with yellow labels marked 'Gas' in black letters at intervals of no more than 5 ft. Labels aren't required on piping in the same room as the appliance it serves.
Steel gas pipe must be at least Schedule 40 (standard weight). Copper tubing may not be used if the gas contains more than an average of 0.3 grains of hydrogen sulfide per 100 standard cubic feet.
Corrugated stainless steel tubing (CSST) must be listed to ANSI LC 1/CSA 6.26 and installed per the manufacturer's instructions.

CSST gas piping must be electrically continuous and bonded to the electrical service grounding electrode system (or lightning protection electrode system) with a bonding conductor at least 6 AWG copper (or equivalent aluminum), no longer than 75 ft.
facts.note: Section was 310.1.1 in the 2015/2018 IFGC. ICC CodeNotes (2021) cites 310.2.

facts.fact: The CSST bonding clamp attaches downstream of the point of delivery (the gas meter or LP second-stage regulator) to rigid pipe, a malleable iron fitting, a manifold or a brass CSST fitting, never to the corrugated tubing itself. One attachment point is enough for the whole system, and the clamp must be listed to UL 467.

Arc-resistant CSST (black jacket marked 'AR', listed to CSA/ANSI LC 1) can rely on the equipment grounding conductor of the appliance circuit instead of a separate bonding jumper. It still needs the direct bond if any yellow CSST is in the system or no connected appliance has an equipment grounding conductor.
facts.note: Per ICC 2021 CodeNotes on CSST.

facts.fact: Above-ground gas piping other than CSST that could become energized must be bonded. It is considered bonded when connected to appliances that are connected to the circuit's equipment grounding conductor.
Gas piping may not be used as a grounding electrode.

Where gas piping other than black or galvanized steel runs through holes or notches less than 1-1/2 in from the edge of wood framing, it must be protected by steel shield plates at least 0.0575 in thick (No. 16 gauge). The plates must extend at least 4 in above sole plates, below top plates and to each side of the member.
facts.note: Note: the IPC requires only 2 in extension for water and drain piping.

facts.fact: Underground gas piping must be buried at least 12 in below grade. Individual lines to outdoor lights, grills or similar appliances may be 8 in deep if approved and not exposed to physical damage.

Plastic gas pipe may be installed only outdoors underground, not inside or under buildings or slabs. It is limited to 100 psig for natural gas and 30 psig for LP-gas. It may come above ground outside only in anodeless or service-head risers, and may run under outdoor patio, walkway and driveway slabs at proper burial depth.

Underground nonmetallic (plastic) gas piping needs a yellow insulated copper tracer wire (at least 18 AWG, rated for direct burial) or other approved conductor laid next to it, accessible or terminating above ground at each end.
Underground gas piping through an outer foundation or basement wall below grade must be encased in a protective sleeve (or otherwise protected), with the annular spaces sealed.
Gas piping pressure tests must use air, nitrogen, carbon dioxide or an inert gas. Oxygen may never be used.

Gas test pressure is read with a manometer or a gauge that can show leakage during the test. A mechanical gauge's full scale may not exceed five times the test pressure, and the pressure source must be isolated before the test.
Gas piping test pressure must be at least 1-1/2 times the maximum working pressure, and never less than 3 psig, regardless of design pressure.
facts.note: Confirmed in 2018 IFGC text. No 2021 change listed.

facts.fact: Gas pressure tests last at least 1/2 hour for each 500 cu ft of pipe volume (or fraction). Systems under 10 cu ft and single-family dwellings may be tested for as little as 10 minutes, and no test needs to exceed 24 hours.

During a gas pressure test, appliances rated for less than the test pressure must be disconnected and their outlets capped. Appliances rated at or above the test pressure may be isolated by closing their shutoff valves.

Gas leaks may never be located with matches, candles, open flames or other ignition sources. Use a noncorrosive leak-detection fluid or approved detector. Minor repairs and additions may be leak-checked that way instead of pressure-tested, if inspected.

Where an appliance has no built-in sediment trap, one must be installed downstream of the appliance shutoff valve as close to the appliance inlet as practical. It is typically a tee with a capped nipple in the bottom opening. Illuminating appliances, ranges, clothes dryers, decorative vented appliances, gas fireplaces and outdoor grills don't need one.
Gas piping for other than dry gas must slope at least 1/4 in in 15 ft to prevent traps.
Each appliance needs its own accessible shutoff valve in the same room, within 6 ft of the appliance, upstream of the union, connector or quick-disconnect it serves.

Appliance connectors must be listed to ANSI Z21.24/CSA 6.10, may not exceed 6 ft in overall length, and only one connector is allowed per appliance. Connectors may not be concealed in or run through walls, floors, partitions, ceilings or appliance housings, and must be in the same room as the appliance.
facts.note: Rigid metallic pipe sized as part of the system may be longer.

facts.fact: Gas pipe support spacing: steel pipe 1/2 in = 6 ft; 3/4 in or 1 in = 8 ft; 1-1/4 in and larger = 10 ft horizontal (every floor level vertical). Smooth-wall tubing 1/2 in = 4 ft; 5/8 in or 3/4 in = 6 ft; 7/8 in or 1 in = 8 ft horizontal. CSST follows the manufacturer.

Standard method for indoor combustion air: the space needs at least 50 cu ft of volume per 1,000 Btu/h of total appliance input. Where infiltration is known to be under 0.40 air changes per hour, the known-infiltration method must be used instead.

When combining indoor spaces on the same story, each opening needs at least 1 sq in of free area per 1,000 Btu/h (minimum 100 sq in), one within 12 in of the top and one within 12 in of the bottom, with no dimension under 3 in. Spaces on different stories need 2 sq in per 1,000 Btu/h.

Outdoor combustion air, two-opening method: one opening within 12 in of the top and one within 12 in of the bottom. Openings direct to outdoors or through vertical ducts need 1 sq in per 4,000 Btu/h each. Openings through horizontal ducts need 1 sq in per 2,000 Btu/h each.

Outdoor combustion air, one-opening method: one opening within 12 in of the top, at least 1 sq in per 3,000 Btu/h and no smaller than the total vent connector area. The appliance needs at least 1 in clearance at the sides and back and 6 in at the front.
Where louver free area is unknown, assume wood louvers have 25% free area and metal louvers or grilles have 75%. Screens over combustion air openings must be no smaller than 1/4 in mesh.

Worked example: an 80,000 Btu/h furnace plus a 40,000 Btu/h water heater = 120,000 Btu/h. Indoor air by the standard method needs 120 x 50 = 6,000 cu ft of room volume. Two direct outdoor openings would each need 120,000 / 4,000 = 30 sq in of free area.
facts.note: Calculation example.

facts.fact: Fuel-burning appliances may not be located in sleeping rooms, bathrooms, toilet rooms, storage closets or surgical rooms (or spaces opening only into them). Exceptions include direct-vent appliances, and properly listed unvented room heaters with oxygen depletion safety shutoff up to 6,000 Btu/h in a bathroom or 10,000 Btu/h in a bedroom.
Vent connectors must have no dips or sags and must slope upward toward the vent or chimney at least 1/4 in per ft.
The maximum horizontal length of a single-wall vent connector is 75% of the height of the chimney or vent.
A Type B gas vent must terminate at least 5 ft in vertical height above the highest connected appliance draft hood or flue collar.
Typical gas supply pressures at appliances: natural gas about 7 in water column (manifold about 3.5 in w.c.), LP-gas about 11 in w.c. 1 psi = 27.7 in w.c.
facts.note: Always follow the appliance rating plate.

facts.fact: Trenches 4 ft or deeper need a stairway, ladder, ramp or other safe exit placed so workers travel no more than 25 ft laterally to reach it.

A protective system (sloping, benching, shoring or shielding) is required in excavations 5 ft or deeper, unless entirely in stable rock. Excavations under 5 ft need protection if a competent person sees signs of possible cave-in.

facts.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P App. B
facts.fact: Sloping or benching for excavations deeper than 20 ft must be designed by a registered professional engineer.

facts.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P App. B, Table B-1
facts.fact: Maximum allowable slopes (horizontal:vertical) for excavations under 20 ft: stable rock vertical (90 degrees); Type A soil 3/4:1 (53 degrees); Type B 1:1 (45 degrees); Type C 1-1/2:1 (34 degrees).

facts.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P App. B
facts.fact: A short-term Type A excavation (open 24 hours or less) 12 ft or less deep may be sloped at 1/2:1 (63 degrees).
Without soil classification or another design option, an excavation must be sloped no steeper than 1-1/2 horizontal to 1 vertical (34 degrees), which is the Type C slope.

facts.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P App. A
